intro_en:
"The Karbolet" (the Cockscomb) - that is what hikers call this segment of the Israel National Trail. The reason: the shape of the crest of the wall of the Large Crater (Makhtesh Gadol) in this area. It is one of the high points of the entire Israel National Trail, because of the walking challenges and the beauty of the scenery.
We hike along the rim of the crater, over the tilted rock strata, with views into the interior of the crater and over the surroundings of the crater to the south and east. The descent along Nahal Afran to the Zin Valley is also beautiful and challenging. The stream, dropping steeply through the tilted strata, creates waterfalls and rock pools.

 Nahal Akrabim - Oron (38)
 Nahal Afran - Hod Akev (40)
character_en: Ascents and descents, some of them steep. A long and challenging day of hiking.
pois_en: Har Karbolet. Viewpoints over the Large Crater. Nahal Afran and its rock pools.
important_en: A long and strenuous day of hiking, so it is recommended to start walking early in the morning.
It is very important to arrange water caching in advance at the Nahal Afran or Nahal Mador campsite.
The segment can be split into two days - at Nahal Mador. Further explanation below.
description_en:
We set out from the overnight campsite beside the entrance gate of the Oron phosphate plant, and walk back along Road 206 to the point where the Israel National Trail begins its climb to Har Karbolet.
From the roadside we climb left into a gentle stream channel towards the railway line. The trail passes under the line through a low culvert. After the crossing we continue up the channel; a dark tilted rock layer (flint) marks the entrance into the ribs of the crater wall.
The channel becomes a little narrower and steeper. We climb the channel to a saddle and descend a short channel on the other side to a dirt road. The trail crosses the road and climbs a rock spur to spot height 581, one of the peaks of Har Karbolet. From this point there is a fine 360-degree view.
Opposite, in the centre of the Large Crater, is a small ridge - the Matmor Hills. The ridge is made of hard limestone from the Jurassic period, the oldest rock exposed on the floor of the Large Crater. Looking east, outside the crater, we see the Oron phosphate plant and the mining areas south of it. Phosphate rock is a marine sedimentary rock rich in phosphorus - a chemical element of great importance in life processes - and the plant's products are used mainly to make agricultural fertiliser. The phosphate is mined in open pits and transferred for enrichment in industrial facilities at the Oron plant.
We continue walking on Har Karbolet, perpendicular to the dip of the strata, along the serrated ridgeline. In places the trail runs right along the ridgeline - the "crest of the Karbolet" - a challenging walk with a steep slope on both sides. Where the trail drops below the ridgeline, we walk along a sloping hillside.
After a stretch along the crest of the Karbolet, the trail turns left and enters a channel that has cut into the seam between two tilted strata. On the left, rock ledges jut out at the top of the tilted layer. Until midday, shady corners for a break and a rest can be found here.
When we reach a fork in the channels, we turn right and climb back up a channel to a saddle. On the other side, we descend a channel that is a tributary of Nahal Mador to its confluence with the stream's main channel. We meet a blue-marked trail that runs along Nahal Mador. The Israel National Trail turns right up the channel, with the blue markings.
Note: those who choose to split the segment into two days must turn left at this point with the blue markings, down Nahal Mador, towards the jeep track beside the railway line. The next day, climb back up the stream and continue walking the segment. Water caching must be arranged at the eastern Nahal Mador campsite.
The Israel National Trail climbs with the blue markings to the summit - spot height 688. This is the highest point the segment passes through, with a fine view in all four directions.
The markings accompanying the Israel National Trail change from blue to red, and we set out on the final stretch of walking along the top of the ridge on the crater rim.
At spot height 625, near "Ma'ale Avraham" in the south-western corner of the crater, there is a wonderful view over the Large Crater. At this point the walls on both sides of the crater meet - and the Israel National Trail begins to move away from the crater rim towards the descent to the Zin Valley. Here.
The trail crosses a channel and then a spur, beyond which we begin to descend into the channel of Nahal Afran. Nahal Afran is steep; its channel carves its course through tilted layers of hard limestone, creating waterfalls and rock pools.
The trail passes through the pools, and at several points handholds and iron steps have been installed to help hikers. Note: it may be necessary to wade through water, depending on recent rains.
As the stream leaves the ribs of the Hatira Ridge, the steep and challenging section of the trail comes to an end. From here, the stream cuts through chalk and flint in gentle terrain until it emerges into the open expanse. On the left we see Givat Mador - an outlier, or isolated hill, that is, a kind of lone island standing out in the landscape. The upper layer of the hill is made of hard limestone, which has protected the softer layers beneath it from erosion. Around it, the corresponding rock layers of the same age and the same geological formations have been washed away and removed.
From here, the way to the overnight campsite at Nahal Mador is easy and quick.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
